unit_label: Module A unit 1: Definition of Statistics, Importance and Limitations; Data Collection, Classification and Tabulation

facts.statement: A statistical study has four phases: collecting numerical data from published or unpublished, primary or secondary sources; classifying and tabulating the raw data into groups or classes shown in a table; analysing the tabulated data with formulas and methods suited to the purpose of the study; and interpreting the results by drawing conclusions. Statistics here means quantitative or numerical data that can be used for further calculation.

Statistics is used in business and economics, medicine, weather forecasting, the stock market, sport and banking. In banking, credit policies are decided from statistical analysis of profitability, demand deposits, time deposits, credit ratios, number of customers and other ratios, and the credit policies rest on the application of probability theory.

The functions of statistics: it presents facts in definite form, simplifies complex data, provides techniques of comparison, studies the relationship between two or more variables, helps in formulating policies and helps in forecasting outcomes.
facts.locator: Printed p. 6, section 1.3 Function of Statistics

facts.statement: Limitations of statistics: it does not deal with individual values but with mass data and aggregates; it does not study qualitative or non-numerical data; its results are not exact and are true only on an average in the long run (a sample is taken as a representative of the whole); and the results can be biased when data collection is biased, for example when handled by an inexperienced or dishonest person.
facts.locator: Printed p. 6, section 1.4 Limitations or Demerits of Statistics

facts.statement: A population is the entire collection of observations being studied, from which data may be collected and about which conclusions are drawn. A sample is a part of the population, taken because the whole is too large, costly or time-consuming to study, and is expected to be representative so that valid conclusions about the whole can be drawn from it.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 6-7, section 1.5 Definitions: Population and Sample

facts.statement: A characteristic that varies from one individual to another and can be expressed in numbers is a variate; one that varies but cannot be expressed in numbers is an attribute. A variate that takes only distinct, countable values (usually a finite number) is a discrete variable, for example the number of members in a family; one that can take any value within a range, integral or fractional, is a continuous variable, for example height or weight.
facts.locator: Printed p. 7, section 1.5 Definitions: Variates and Attributes

facts.statement: A parameter is a numerical value or function of the observations of the whole population; it is usually unknown but fixed (population mean, median, standard deviation). Because it is unknown it is estimated from a sample using a statistic, a quantity or function of the sample observations; the sample mean estimates the population mean. A statistic is also called an estimator.
facts.locator: Printed p. 7, section 1.5 Definitions: Parameter and Statistic

facts.statement: Primary data is collected directly, for the first time, by the investigator from respondents, by methods such as direct interview (face-to-face contact with respondents who are asked questions) and questionnaires (instruments with closed-ended or open-ended questions, now often administered online). Secondary data already exists and was collected earlier by some agency for another purpose, and comes from published or unpublished sources such as records, research and educational organisations, banks, financial institutions, magazines and the internet.

Primary data in the hands of one person can be secondary for everyone else (a census report is primary for the Registrar General and secondary for others). Primary data is original and so more accurate, but collecting it needs more money, time and energy than using secondary data, so the choice between the two should be made carefully.
facts.locator: Printed p. 8, Distinction between primary and secondary data

facts.statement: In a census, data are collected about every individual unit of the population; in a survey, data are collected about only a part of it, called the sample, and used to estimate the characteristics of the whole, so the sample has to be representative of the population (for example in its age and gender proportions).
facts.locator: Printed p. 8, Census and sample survey

facts.statement: Classification arranges raw data into homogeneous groups or classes according to common characteristics, which condenses the data, makes it easier to compare, and leads to tabulation. The four bases are qualitative (a quality or attribute), quantitative (a numerical characteristic such as income or age), geographical (region or location) and chronological or temporal (time of occurrence, also called time series data). By the number of characteristics used at once, classification is one-way (one), two-way (two) or multi-way (more than two).
facts.locator: Printed p. 9, section 1.7 Classification and Tabulation

facts.statement: Frequency is the number of times a value of a variable occurs in a series of observations, and a frequency distribution is a table that lists values or classes of the variable with their frequencies; classes are normally of equal size and cover the range of the observations. For a class, the lower and upper values are its class limits, class length (width) = upper limit - lower limit, and class mark (mid-value) = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 9-10, section 1.8 Frequency Distribution, items 1 to 3

facts.statement: Class intervals are exclusive when the upper limit is excluded from the class and counted in the next one (in the courseware example a value of 15 is excluded from the class 10-15 and counted in the class 15-20), and inclusive when both limits belong to the class (60-69, 70-79). An inclusive class series is converted to an exclusive one, giving class boundaries, by subtracting half the gap between classes from each lower limit and adding it to each upper limit: for 5-9 and 10-14 the gap is 1, so the boundaries are 4.5-9.5 and 9.5-14.5.

An open-end class has either the lower limit of the first class or the upper limit of the last class, or both, missing (for example Below 10 or Above 40). Relative frequency = class frequency / total frequency; percentage frequency = (class frequency / total frequency) x 100; frequency density = class frequency / class width.

A discrete frequency distribution lists the distinct values the variable takes with their frequencies; a continuous frequency distribution groups values into class intervals. A cumulative frequency distribution is of two types: the less-than type adds frequencies from the lowest class upwards, and the greater-than (more-than) type adds them from the highest class downwards.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 11-13, section 1.8 and Problems 1 to 5

payload.title: What a statistical study does with data
payload.core_explanation_md:
A statistical study turns a pile of numbers into a decision in four steps, always in this order:

| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Collect | Gather numerical data from the right source |
| Classify and tabulate | Sort the raw data into groups and show it in a table |
| Analyse | Apply formulas and methods that suit the question |
| Interpret | Draw conclusions from the results |

Why bother? Statistics does six jobs: it states facts in definite form, simplifies complicated data, gives a way of comparing, studies how two or more variables move together, supports policy making and helps forecast.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The word "statistics" here means numerical (quantitative) data that can feed further calculation. If a step is skipped, the later ones suffer: analysis done on badly classified data gives a neat-looking but meaningless answer.

self_check.prompt_text: From memory: list the four phases of a statistical study in order, and name three of the six functions of statistics.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Collect, classify and tabulate, analyse, interpret. Functions: present facts definitely, simplify data, compare, study relationships between variables, help in policy making, help in forecasting (any three).

payload.title: Statistics in banking, and where it stops
payload.core_explanation_md:
Banks lean on statistics because their decisions rest on large numbers of accounts and transactions. Credit policy, for example, is set after studying profitability, demand and time deposits, credit ratios and customer numbers, and the policy itself rests on probability theory.

Four limits keep this honest:

- **Aggregates, not individuals.** Statistics describes groups; it says little about one particular borrower.
- **Numbers only.** Purely qualitative facts must first be turned into numbers before statistics can handle them.
- **Averages, not certainties.** Results are true on average over the long run, because a sample stands in for the whole.
- **Bias in, bias out.** Careless or dishonest data collection ruins the whole investigation.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A useful habit: before trusting a statistical claim, ask who collected the data and how. The first three limits are built into the method; the fourth is a failure of people.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager says "statistics proves that this borrower will default". Which limitation of statistics does that statement ignore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Statistics deals with aggregates and long-run averages, not with individual cases; it can say how likely default is across a group, not what one borrower will do.

payload.title: Population and sample, parameter and statistic
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two pairs of words carry most of this unit.

| Group-wide | Part-wide |
| --- | --- |
| **Population**: every observation you want to draw conclusions about | **Sample**: a part of the population actually studied |
| **Parameter**: a number describing the population (fixed, usually unknown) | **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter |

Example in a bank: the population is the balances of all savings accounts in a region. Average balance of all of them is a parameter. If you look at 400 accounts and compute their average, that average is a statistic, and you use it to estimate the unknown parameter.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: We sample because the population is often too large, too costly or too slow to study in full. The sample must be representative, otherwise the statistic will mislead about the parameter. A statistic is also called an estimator.

self_check.prompt_text: You compute the average loan size of 250 randomly picked accounts out of 40,000. Is the result a parameter or a statistic, and what does it estimate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is a statistic. It estimates the parameter: the average loan size of all 40,000 accounts.

payload.title: Attributes, variates, discrete and continuous
payload.core_explanation_md:
Ask one question of any characteristic: *can it be written as a number?*

- No: it is an **attribute** (type of account, branch location, religion, colour).
- Yes: it is a **variate** (balance, age, number of dependants). A variate is then split by the values it can take:

| Kind of variate | Takes | Banking examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discrete | Separate, countable values | Number of loan accounts a customer holds; cheques returned in a month |
| Continuous | Any value in a range, whole or fractional | Account balance in rupees and paise; time taken to process a loan |

Counting gives discrete data; measuring gives continuous data.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Watch out for rounded measurements. Age is continuous in principle, even though it is often reported in whole years; the courseware lists "age in years" as discrete, so read the question for how the variable is being recorded.

self_check.prompt_text: Classify each: (a) type of deposit scheme, (b) number of ATMs in a district, (c) time a customer waits at the counter.

payload.title: Primary or secondary data, census or survey
payload.core_explanation_md:
Data comes from one of two places, and is collected on one of two scales.

| | Primary data | Secondary data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collected | First time, directly from respondents | Earlier, by someone else, for another purpose |
| Usual methods or sources | Direct interview, questionnaires | Records, published reports, banks, research bodies, the internet |
| Cost in money, time, effort | Higher | Lower |
| Fit to your question | Designed for it | Must be checked |

The same figures can be primary for one user and secondary for another: a statistical table is primary for the office that gathered it and secondary for the analyst who reuses it.

On scale: a **census** covers every unit of the population, while a **sample survey** covers a part and generalises to the whole, which works only if the sample is representative.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Choosing is a trade-off. If a good secondary source already answers the question, using it saves money and time. If it does not fit, primary collection is worth its cost.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank wants customer opinion on a new app feature. Would you start with primary or secondary data, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Primary data (for example a questionnaire), because existing records will not hold opinions on a feature the customers have only just seen.

payload.title: Classifying data: four bases and how many ways
payload.core_explanation_md:
Classification sorts raw data into groups that share a characteristic. It shrinks a long list into a few classes you can compare, and it is the step before tabulation.

**Base** (what you sort by):

| Base | Sorted by | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qualitative | A quality or attribute | Deposit accounts by type of scheme |
| Quantitative | A numerical characteristic | Borrowers by loan amount |
| Geographical | Place | Deposits by state |
| Chronological | Time of occurrence | Quarter-wise gross NPAs (a time series) |

**Number of ways** (how many characteristics at once): one characteristic is *one-way*, two is *two-way* and more than two is *multi-way*.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A table with branch type down the side and account type across the top is a two-way classification. Adding a third characteristic, such as year, makes it multi-way.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the base and the number of ways: customers classified by city and by gender.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Geographical and qualitative bases, classified two-way.

payload.title: Class width, class mark and class boundaries
payload.core_explanation_md:
Each class in a frequency table has a lower limit and an upper limit. Two quantities describe it:

- the **width** says how big the class is;
- the **class mark** is the middle of the class, used to stand for every value in it.

In an **exclusive** series (0-10, 10-20, ...) a value equal to the upper limit is counted in the next class. In an **inclusive** series (60-69, 70-79, ...) both limits belong to the class. To get continuous classes from an inclusive series, widen each class by half the gap between one upper limit and the next lower limit: these are the **class boundaries**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: If you are asked for a class width when only the data are given, divide the range (largest minus smallest value) by the number of classes wanted. Boundaries are what make inclusive classes safe to use in calculations that treat the variable as continuous.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{width} = U - L,\quad m = \frac{L + U}{2},\quad L_b = L - \frac{g}{2},\quad U_b = U + \frac{g}{2}

variables.name: Gap between the upper limit of one inclusive class and the lower limit of the next

assumptions: For width and mark, use the limits of the class as given (exclusive) or its boundaries (inclusive); both give the same width and mark for equal-width inclusive classes.
Classes of equal width cover the observed range without a break.
common_errors: Using 1 instead of half the gap when widening inclusive limits (the adjustment is half of the gap, so 0.5 for a gap of 1).
Counting a value equal to an upper limit in the lower class of an exclusive series.
Subtracting limits of an inclusive class to get the width (9 - 5 = 4) instead of using boundaries (9.5 - 4.5 = 5).

self_check.prompt_text: Inclusive classes run 1-5, 6-10, 11-15. Give the boundaries of the middle class and its mark.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Gap is 1, so adjust by 0.5: boundaries 5.5 to 10.5; mark (6 + 10)/2 = 8.

payload.title: Relative, percentage frequency and frequency density
payload.core_explanation_md:
Raw class frequencies are hard to compare across tables of different sizes, so express each as a share of the total:

- **Relative frequency** is a fraction of 1;
- **Percentage frequency** is the same share out of 100.

When classes have unequal widths, a bigger class naturally collects more observations. **Frequency density** removes that effect by dividing by width, so you can see where observations really crowd together.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Relative frequencies of all classes add to 1 (or to 100 for percentages), which is a handy check on your arithmetic. Density only matters when widths differ; with equal widths it just rescales the frequencies.

variables.name: Relative frequency, percentage frequency, frequency density
variables.unit: fraction, per cent, observations per unit of the variable

assumptions: N is the sum of all class frequencies in the table.
Width is measured in the same unit for every class.
common_errors: Dividing by the number of classes instead of the total frequency.
Forgetting the factor 100 for the percentage frequency.
Comparing raw frequencies of classes of different widths instead of their densities.

self_check.prompt_text: A class holds 18 of 75 observations. What are its relative and percentage frequencies?

payload.title: Cumulative frequencies: less-than and more-than
payload.core_explanation_md:
A cumulative frequency answers "how many observations are at or below this point?" or "at or above?" without adding up the table each time.

| Type | How it is built | What the last or first entry shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Less-than | Add class frequencies from the lowest class upwards | The final entry equals the total |
| More-than (greater-than) | Add them from the highest class downwards | The first entry equals the total |

The two always pair up: the less-than count at a boundary plus the more-than count at the same boundary give the total.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Each cumulative value is tied to a class boundary, not to a class. "Less than 30" means everything below the boundary 30.

self_check.prompt_text: Classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 have frequencies 5, 9, 6. Write the less-than cumulative frequencies.

payload.title: Turning loan-size classes into boundaries and class marks
payload.core_explanation_md: A bank groups fifty new term loans by size in ₹ lakh using inclusive classes 1-5, 6-10, 11-15 and 16-20, with frequencies 8, 20, 12, 10. Convert the classes to boundaries, find the class width and the mark of each class.

worked_steps.description: Find the gap between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
Half the gap is the adjustment.
Subtract it from each lower limit and add it to each upper limit.
Width of any class from its boundaries.
Class marks from the original limits.
Check that the frequencies add to the loans counted.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Boundaries 0.5-5.5, 5.5-10.5, 10.5-15.5, 15.5-20.5 (₹ lakh); width ₹5 lakh; class marks ₹3, 8, 13 and 18 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: Why do the boundaries, not the limits, let us treat loan size as continuous?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the boundaries leave no gaps: 5.5 belongs to the end of one class and the start of the next, so every possible loan size, such as ₹5.7 lakh, falls in exactly one class.

payload.title: Shares, density and cumulative counts for savings balances
payload.core_explanation_md: A bank samples 120 savings accounts and groups the average balance (₹ thousand) in exclusive classes of unequal width: 0-10 (40 accounts), 10-20 (36), 20-40 (30) and 40-80 (14). Find the percentage frequency and frequency density of each class, and both cumulative frequencies.

worked_steps.description: Percentage frequency of each class: frequency / 120 x 100, to 2 decimals.
Less-than cumulative frequencies, adding from the lowest class.
More-than cumulative frequencies, adding from the highest class.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 120, 80, 44, 14 (for the classes taken lowest to highest)

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Percentage frequencies 33.33, 30.00, 25.00, 11.67 (sum 100.00); densities 4.00, 3.60, 1.50, 0.35 accounts per ₹ thousand; less-than 40, 76, 106, 120; more-than 120, 80, 44, 14

self_check.prompt_text: Which class has the most accounts per ₹ thousand of balance, and why is that different from the class with the most accounts?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The 0-10 class has the highest density (4.00); here it is also the largest class, but the 40-80 class shows how a wide class can hold many accounts while being thinly populated (density 0.35).

payload.title: From a raw list to a discrete frequency distribution
payload.core_explanation_md: The number of loan accounts held by each of 20 sampled customers is: 2, 1, 3, 2, 2, 4, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 4, 3, 2. Build the frequency distribution and the less-than cumulative frequency, and say how many customers hold at most two accounts.

worked_steps.description: List the distinct values in order.

worked_steps.formula_or_substitution: count of each value in the list

worked_steps.description: Customers holding at most two accounts: frequencies of 1 and 2.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: 13 of 20 customers hold at most two loan accounts

self_check.prompt_text: Why is this a discrete rather than a continuous frequency distribution?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The variable (number of accounts) takes only separate whole values, so each value gets its own row instead of being grouped into a class interval.

payload.stem_md: Which description fits "the number of dependants in a borrower's household"?

options.text_md: An attribute, because a household is a group of people
options.explanation_md: Dependants are counted, so the characteristic can be written as a number; an attribute cannot.

options.text_md: A continuous variate, because it can be any value
options.explanation_md: The count can only be whole numbers, 0, 1, 2 and so on, not any value in a range.

options.text_md: A discrete variate, because it takes separate countable values
options.explanation_md: A count of people takes distinct whole-number values, which is the definition of a discrete variate.

options.text_md: A parameter, because it describes the whole population
options.explanation_md: A parameter is a summary of a population, not a kind of characteristic.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A characteristic that can be expressed in numbers is a variate, and one that takes only separate, countable values is discrete. Dependants are counted in whole numbers.

payload.stem_md: A bank records the location type of each branch as rural, semi-urban, urban or metropolitan. In statistical terms this characteristic is

options.text_md: a discrete variate
options.explanation_md: Location type is not expressed in numbers, so it is not a variate of any kind.

options.text_md: an attribute
options.explanation_md: It varies from branch to branch but is described in words, not numbers.

options.text_md: a continuous variate
options.explanation_md: Nothing is measured on a scale here.

options.text_md: a statistic
options.explanation_md: A statistic is a number computed from a sample, not a characteristic.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A characteristic that varies between individuals but cannot be expressed in numbers is an attribute.

payload.stem_md: From 3,20,000 savings accounts a bank draws 500 at random and finds an average balance of ₹18,400. What is ₹18,400?

options.text_md: A parameter of the population of savings accounts
options.explanation_md: A parameter describes the whole population; this figure comes from only part of it.

options.text_md: The population mean
options.explanation_md: The population mean would need all 3,20,000 balances.

options.text_md: A census value
options.explanation_md: A census covers every unit; only 500 of them were examined.

options.text_md: A statistic, usable as an estimate of the population mean
options.explanation_md: It is computed from a sample, so it is a statistic, and the sample mean is used to estimate the unknown population mean.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A quantity computed from sample observations is a statistic. It is used to estimate the corresponding, usually unknown, population parameter.

payload.stem_md: An analyst studying deposit growth downloads a statistical table already compiled and published by another organisation. For this analyst the data is

options.text_md: Primary, because the analyst is using it for the first time
options.explanation_md: Primary data is collected first-hand by the investigator; first use by the analyst does not make it primary.

options.text_md: Primary, because the table contains numbers
options.explanation_md: The presence of numbers does not decide the type; the source of collection does.

options.text_md: Secondary, because someone else collected it earlier for their own purpose
options.explanation_md: The data already existed and was collected by another agency, which is the meaning of secondary data. It may have been primary for the compiler.

options.text_md: Neither, because published data is a census
options.explanation_md: A census is a way of covering a population, not a type of source.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Data collected earlier by someone else is secondary for everyone who reuses it, even if it was primary for the organisation that collected it.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is a census rather than a sample survey?

options.text_md: Calling 400 customers chosen at random from the 2 lakh on the books
options.explanation_md: Only a part of the population is covered.

options.text_md: Reading every one of the 1,150 safe-deposit locker agreements held by a branch
options.explanation_md: Every unit of the population (all lockers at the branch) is covered, which is a census of that population.

options.text_md: Asking customers who visit on a Monday to fill a questionnaire
options.explanation_md: Only the Monday visitors are covered, which is a part of the population.

options.text_md: Reviewing 50 loan files chosen from each region
options.explanation_md: A part of the files is reviewed, so it is a sample.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A census collects data about every unit of the population being studied; the other options each examine only a part of it.

payload.stem_md: Which question lies outside what statistical methods are good at answering?

options.text_md: What share of the bank's term loans became overdue last year?
options.explanation_md: This describes an aggregate and is well suited to statistics.

options.text_md: How are average deposits related to the number of branches over the years?
options.explanation_md: The relationship between variables is a standard statistical task.

options.text_md: Will this particular borrower, whose file is open on the desk, repay on time?
options.explanation_md: Statistics deals with groups and long-run averages, not with the certain outcome for one individual.

options.text_md: What will the likely trend in card spending be next year?
options.explanation_md: Forecasting from data is one of the functions of statistics.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Statistics works with aggregates and long-run averages. It can describe how likely repayment is across a group of similar borrowers, but cannot settle what one individual will do.

payload.stem_md: Which sequence gives the phases of a statistical study in the correct order?

options.text_md: Collect, analyse, classify and tabulate, interpret
options.explanation_md: Data has to be classified and tabulated before it is analysed.

options.text_md: Classify and tabulate, collect, analyse, interpret
options.explanation_md: Data has to be collected before it can be classified.

options.text_md: Collect, classify and tabulate, interpret, analyse
options.explanation_md: Conclusions are drawn only after the analysis is done.

options.text_md: Collect, classify and tabulate, analyse, interpret
options.explanation_md: This is the order: gather the data, organise it, apply methods to it, then draw conclusions.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The four phases are collection, classification and tabulation, analysis and interpretation, in that order.

payload.stem_md: A bank presents its gross NPA ratio for each of the last eight quarters. On which base is this data classified?

options.text_md: Chronological, because it is arranged by time of occurrence
options.explanation_md: Data arranged by quarters, years or months is classified on a time basis and is called a time series.

options.text_md: Geographical, because the bank has branches in many places
options.explanation_md: The data is ordered by time, not by place.

options.text_md: Qualitative, because NPAs are a quality issue
options.explanation_md: The ratio is a number and the grouping is by quarter, not by an attribute.

options.text_md: Quantitative, because it is a ratio
options.explanation_md: A quantitative base would group by the size of a numerical value, not by when it occurred.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Data arranged by the time at which it occurred (years, quarters, months) uses the chronological base and is called time series data.

payload.stem_md: A table shows the number of customers by type of account (savings, current, term deposit) and, at the same time, by gender. This is

options.text_md: One-way classification
options.explanation_md: One-way uses a single characteristic; this table uses two.

options.text_md: Multi-way classification with at least three characteristics
options.explanation_md: Only two characteristics are used, not more than two.

options.text_md: Chronological classification
options.explanation_md: There is no time element in the table.

options.text_md: Two-way classification
options.explanation_md: Two characteristics, account type and gender, are used at the same time.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Classifying by two characteristics at once is two-way classification; one is one-way and more than two is multi-way.

payload.stem_md: In the exclusive classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 and 30-40, an account with a balance of exactly 20 (₹ thousand) is counted in

options.text_md: The class 10-20, because 20 is its upper limit
options.explanation_md: In an exclusive series the upper limit is not part of the class.

options.text_md: Both 10-20 and 20-30
options.explanation_md: A value is counted in one class only.

options.text_md: The class 20-30, where 20 is the lower limit
options.explanation_md: The upper limit of a class is excluded and the value goes into the next class.

options.text_md: The class 30-40
options.explanation_md: The value is not near that class.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Exclusive classes leave out the upper limit, so a value equal to it is counted in the next class. A balance of 20 therefore belongs to 20-30.

payload.stem_md: Which of these frequency classes is open-ended?

options.explanation_md: Both limits are given.

options.text_md: Above 40
options.explanation_md: The upper limit is missing, which makes the class open-ended.
Both limits are given.
Both limits are given.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An open-end class lacks the lower limit of the first class, the upper limit of the last class, or both.

payload.stem_md: In a more-than (greater-than) cumulative frequency table built from classes listed lowest to highest, the entry against the lowest class equals

options.text_md: The frequency of the lowest class alone
options.explanation_md: That is the frequency, not the cumulative value.

options.text_md: The total frequency, because every observation is at or above the lowest boundary
options.explanation_md: More-than frequencies are added from the highest class downwards, so by the lowest class everything has been added.

options.text_md: Zero
options.explanation_md: Nothing has been left out below the lowest class.

options.text_md: The frequency of the highest class
options.explanation_md: That is the first value added, not the lowest class entry.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The more-than cumulative frequency adds from the highest class downward, so the lowest class carries the total.

payload.stem_md: Daily cash balances run from a smallest value of ₹210 thousand to a largest of ₹1,250 thousand. The bank wants equal-width classes of ₹130 thousand each, starting at the smallest value. How many classes are needed to cover the whole range?
payload.correct_explanation_md: The range is 1,250 - 210 = 1,040. Dividing by the class width, 1,040 / 130 = 8 classes.

payload.stem_md: The inclusive classes for ages of borrowers are 30-39, 40-49, 50-59. What is the class mark of the class 40-49?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 1 decimal place.

payload.stem_md: Customers are grouped by monthly turnover (₹ thousand) in inclusive classes 100-199, 200-299 and 300-399. What is the lower class boundary of the class 200-299?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 1 decimal place.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The gap between 199 and 200 is 1, half of it is 0.5, and 200 - 0.5 = 199.5.

worked_solution_steps.description: Subtract half the gap from the lower limit.

payload.stem_md: In a table of 75 observations a class has frequency 18. What is its percentage frequency?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.stem_md: A class of width ₹20 thousand holds 30 accounts. What is its frequency density, in accounts per ₹ thousand?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Frequency density = class frequency / class width = 30 / 20 = 1.50.
